root_cause.text: The Tegra124 EMC timing-change logic in `tegra124_emc_prepare_timing_change()` misinterpreted the `emc_mode_1` A0 bit semantics, treating bit 0 set as DLL enabled even though DLL is enabled when A0 is clear, causing reversed `dll_change` state selection.
root_cause.evidence: The patch changes `else if (timing->emc_mode_1 & 0x1)` to `else if (!(timing->emc_mode_1 & 0x1))`, and both the CVE and commit message explicitly state that “the code checking whether the specified memory timing enables DLL in the EMRS register was reversed” and that “DLL is enabled if bit A0 is low.”

intent_record.intent_summary: Fix inverted DLL transition detection so EMC timing changes assign DLL on/off actions based on the correct `emc_mode_1` bit state.
intent_record.what: The conditional branch determining `dll_change` was modified by negating the test on `timing->emc_mode_1 & 0x1`, changing `else if (timing->emc_mode_1 & 0x1)` to `else if (!(timing->emc_mode_1 & 0x1))`.
intent_record.how: This reverses which EMC mode transition is classified as `DLL_CHANGE_ON` versus falling through to `DLL_CHANGE_OFF` when bit 0 of `emc_mode_1` changes, correcting the runtime selection of DLL state change handling during timing transitions.

candidates.rationale: This condition embodies the root cause by interpreting bit 0 set as meaning the DLL is enabled, which is backwards for Tegra124 where the DLL is enabled when A0 is clear. That inverted test directly causes DLL_CHANGE_ON/OFF to be selected in reverse.
This assignment becomes wrong because it is reached when the buggy condition treats emc_mode_1 bit 0 set as DLL enabled. It directly encodes the reversed transition state.
This assignment is the opposite half of the inversion bug: when bit 0 is actually clear and DLL should be considered enabled, execution falls here and incorrectly marks the transition as DLL off.

vuln_statements.explanation: This conditional is the root cause: it interprets bit 0 of emc_mode_1 being set as the DLL-enabled case, but on Tegra124 the DLL is enabled when A0/bit 0 is clear. That inverted test causes the subsequent DLL change state selection to be reversed.

bic_trace_step.reason: The provided function body for `tegra_emc_prepare_timing_change()` is sufficient because it directly contains the `emc_mode_1` bit-0 interpretation and the resulting `dll_change` selection logic. The vulnerable construct is present in the initial DLL state computation: `if ((last->emc_mode_1 & 0x1) == (timing->emc_mode_1 & 0x1)) dll_change = DLL_CHANGE_NONE; else if (timing->emc_mode_1 & 0x1) dll_change = DLL_CHANGE_ON; else dll_change = DLL_CHANGE_OFF;`. Per the stated root cause, A0/bit 0 semantics are inverted: DLL is enabled when A0 is clear, not when bit 0 is set. This code explicitly treats `timing->emc_mode_1 & 0x1` as meaning DLL ON, so the `DLL_CHANGE_ON` / `DLL_CHANGE_OFF` states are reversed. Downstream logic then acts on this wrong state, e.g. `if (emc->dram_type == DRAM_TYPE_DDR3 && dll_change == DLL_CHANGE_ON)` for long wait prediction, `if (emc->dram_type == DRAM_TYPE_DDR3 && dll_change == DLL_CHANGE_OFF)` for 'Turn off DLL and enter self-refresh', and `if ((timing->emc_mode_reset != last->emc_mode_reset) || dll_change == DLL_CHANGE_ON)` where DLL reset bits are set. There is no corrected inversion such as testing for bit clear (`!(timing->emc_mode_1 & 0x1)`) anywhere in this logic, so the fix is not present.
